speaker: PROFESSOR
text: Chapter 2. The Beautiful Failure of Classical Robotics.

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: Classical robotics is built on a beautiful idea: if you know the physics, you can compute the motion. Want to move a robot arm to a specific point? Just solve the equations.

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: If forward kinematics is "given angles, find position"... what if you need to do it backwards? Given a target position, which angles should you use?

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: This is inverse kinematics (IK), and it's where the elegance starts to crack.

speaker: STUDENT_1
text: What is classical robotics and what approach does it take?

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: Classical robotics uses explicit mathematical models - kinematics (geometry of motion) and dynamics (forces) - to calculate exactly how a robot should move. It's deterministic: same input always gives same output.

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: For example, with your SO-ARM101: Classical approach would calculate SO-ARM101's joint angles using transformation matrices, but this breaks down when fabric deforms unpredictably.

speaker: STUDENT_1
text: So classical robotics is all about deriving equations from physics - if you know the math perfectly, you know exactly where the arm will go.

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: Exactly. It works beautifully in controlled factory settings.

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: Engineers spent decades perfecting these equations, only to find that real-world uncertainty defeats mathematical elegance every time.

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: Unlike FK, IK often has multiple solutions - or no solution at all. Your robot might be able to reach a point with its elbow up or elbow down. Or the point might be outside its reach entirely. Suddenly, simple trigonometry becomes a constrained optimization problem.

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: Your SO-ARM101 has 6 joints per arm. For FK, you chain 6 transformation matrices together - still manageable. But for IK? With 6 joints, you're solving a system with multiple solutions, joint limits, and singularities (positions where the math breaks down). Now imagine coordinating two arms for bimanual manipulation...

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: Consider a simple pendulum. The equation of motion is textbook physics:

speaker: STUDENT_2
text: What are equations of motion in robotics?

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: Mathematical relationships mapping joint configurations (angles, velocities) to end-effector positions and forces. They describe how the robot's state evolves over time based on applied torques.

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: For SO-ARM101's 6-DOF arm, equations of motion relate the 6 joint angles to where the gripper ends up in 3D space (x, y, z, roll, pitch, yaw).

speaker: STUDENT_3
text: So these equations let you predict exactly where the arm will be if you know the joint angles?

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: In theory, yes. The reality is messier.

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: NASA's robotic arms on the Space Station use these exact equations - but they operate in a perfectly known, zero-gravity environment.

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: That beautiful equation ignores: air resistance (the pendulum doesn't swing in a vacuum), joint friction (the pivot point has drag), material deformation (the rod isn't perfectly rigid), and temperature effects (metal expands, lubricant viscosity changes). The real world has infinite hidden variables.

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: This is called undermodeling - your mathematical model doesn't capture enough of reality. And here's the cruel irony: you can't capture enough of reality. The real world is infinitely complex.

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: Now imagine trying to model a robot folding fabric. The cloth deforms unpredictably. Each fold changes the dynamics. The material properties vary across different clothes. You'd need to model every fiber.

speaker: STUDENT_3
text: How does forward kinematics work for a simple 2-link robot arm?

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: Given joint angles theta1 and theta2, calculate end-effector position using: x = L1*cos(theta1) + L2*cos(theta1+theta2), y = L1*sin(theta1) + L2*sin(theta1+theta2). It's just trigonometry.

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: For example, with your SO-ARM101: SO-ARM101 has 6 joints, so FK chains 6 transformation matrices together - each joint adds rotation/translation to get final gripper pose.

speaker: STUDENT_4
text: So forward kinematics is the easy direction - plug in joint angles, get end position. But real robots need to go the other way.

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: Right. And that reverse problem is where classical methods struggle.

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: This is why robot calibration is a whole field - even small errors in link lengths compound into centimeters of end-effector error.

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: 1. The Pipeline Problem: Perception to State Estimation to Planning to Control. If any block fails, errors cascade through the entire system. 2. Multimodal Data: Classical equations can't incorporate camera images, force feedback, and joint angles simultaneously. 3. Undermodeling: You can never capture all real-world variables in equations. 4. Ignoring Data: We have massive robotics datasets now - classical methods don't use any of them.

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: Explicit Modeling (Classical Robotics): You write down equations. Forward kinematics, inverse dynamics, trajectory optimization - everything is derived from first principles. You're explicitly telling the robot how the world works. Implicit Modeling (Learning-Based): No equations. No pipelines. Just a single neural network that takes in observations and outputs actions. The "model" of the world is implicit - learned from data, buried in the network weights. You can't inspect it or debug it, but it captures things equations never could.

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: When your SO-ARM101 grips a t-shirt, the fabric deforms in ways that would take thousands of equations to model explicitly. But if you train on 1000 demonstrations of shirt folding, the implicit model learns "when I see this crinkle pattern, grip here and pull this way." No equations needed - just data.

speaker: STUDENT_4
text: Why don't classical robotics equations work well in real life?

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: Real world has friction, backlash, wear, temperature changes, object deformation, and sensor noise. Mathematical models assume perfect conditions that never exist. The 'undermodeling' gap causes errors to accumulate.

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: Your SO-ARM101 servos have gear backlash and cable stretch not in any equation. Fabric physics are nearly impossible to model - that's why we need learning.

speaker: STUDENT_4
text: So even perfect equations fail because real motors have friction, gears have backlash, and temperature changes everything?

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: Exactly. The map is never the territory.

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: This is why industrial robots need recalibration every few months - gear wear and cable stretch accumulate errors the equations can't predict.

speaker: STUDENT_1
text: What is explicit modeling in robotics?

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: Building mathematical equations that describe exactly how the robot moves - mass, inertia, joint limits, link lengths. You explicitly model every physical property and use physics to compute motion.

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: Explicit model of SO-ARM101 would include each link's mass, servo torque curves, gear ratios, cable elasticity - incredibly complex and never perfectly accurate.

speaker: STUDENT_2
text: So explicit modeling means writing down every physical property - masses, lengths, frictions - and hoping you got them all right.

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: Exactly. Miss one parameter and your predictions drift.

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: Companies spend millions calibrating industrial robots - measuring every parameter precisely - and still need regular recalibration as components wear.

speaker: STUDENT_2
text: What is Forward Kinematics (FK)?

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: FK computes the end-effector pose (position + orientation) given joint angles. Input: joint configuration. Output: where the gripper is in 3D space. It's the 'easy direction' - always has a unique solution.

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: Given SO-ARM101's 6 joint angles (base, shoulder, elbow, wrist1, wrist2, gripper), FK tells you the exact (x, y, z, roll, pitch, yaw) of the gripper.

speaker: STUDENT_1
text: So FK is the easy direction - angles go in, position comes out - because the math is just plugging numbers into known equations?

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: Right. It's purely computational, no search required.

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: Every robot simulator from Gazebo to Isaac Sim implements FK identically - it's the one solved problem in robotics.

speaker: STUDENT_3
text: What is Inverse Kinematics (IK) and why is it harder than FK?

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: IK computes joint angles needed to reach a desired end-effector pose. It's the 'hard direction' - may have multiple solutions, no solutions (unreachable), or require iterative numerical solving.

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: To reach point (30cm, 20cm, 15cm), IK finds joint angles that put SO-ARM101's gripper there. Multiple arm configurations might achieve the same position.

speaker: STUDENT_3
text: So inverse kinematics has multiple solutions - there could be five different ways to reach the same point, and you have to pick one.

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: Right. And picking wrong means hitting yourself or the table.

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: IK solvers are still a bottleneck in animation and games - that's why motion capture exists. It's easier to record human motion than to synthesize it.

speaker: STUDENT_4
text: What are the four main limitations of dynamics-based robotics?

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: 1) Multimodal data is hard to integrate 2) Undermodeling - real physics is more complex 3) Ignores available data 4) Requires separate perception/planning/control modules that don't optimize end-to-end.

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: Classical approach for SO-ARM101 folding would need separate vision module, fabric physics model, motion planner, and controller - each introducing errors.

speaker: STUDENT_2
text: So classical robotics fails because: it can't handle cameras well, reality is too complex to model, data gets wasted, and small errors snowball?

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: Perfect summary. These four walls pushed the field toward learning.

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: Amazon's warehouse robots still fail on unfamiliar packages - their classical perception pipeline breaks on anything it wasn't programmed for.

speaker: STUDENT_1
text: What is the classical robotics pipeline?

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: Perception (understand scene from sensors) to State Estimation (localize robot and objects) to Planning (compute trajectory) to Control (execute motion). Each module is engineered separately.

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: Classical: Camera detects fabric to Estimate fabric pose to Plan fold trajectory to Send joint commands. Each module can fail, and errors compound.

speaker: STUDENT_1
text: So the classical pipeline is like a chain - perception, then planning, then control - and if any link fails, the whole thing breaks.

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: Exactly. Each module's errors compound through the chain.

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: Each stage in this pipeline adds latency and error - by the time you've planned and executed, the world has already changed.

speaker: STUDENT_2
text: What is implicit modeling in robotics?

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: Instead of explicit physics equations, learn a neural network that directly maps observations to actions. The 'model' is implicit in the network weights, learned from data rather than engineered.

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: ACT policy for SO-ARM101 is implicit: (camera + joints) to neural network to actions. No explicit kinematics - the network learns the mapping.

speaker: STUDENT_3
text: So instead of writing physics equations, we let a neural network figure out the physics from examples?

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: Exactly. Learn the function, don't derive it.

speaker: PROFESSOR
text: Tesla's Optimus learned to pick up objects without any physics equations - the neural network figured out the dynamics from watching humans.
